photonics-electronics.name: Integrated photonics and electronics
photonics-electronics.introduction: Electronics computes; light carries information. What happens when their strengths meet?
photonics-electronics.summary: Integrating photonics and electronics brings optical technology together with electronic circuits. Electronics is well suited to computation and control, while light can carry large amounts of information. Bringing them closer aims to improve the speed and energy efficiency of communication within information systems.

sections.title: Why use light?
sections.body: Data centers do more than compute: they move enormous amounts of data between devices and chips. High-speed electrical connections face challenges including transmission losses and heat. Bringing optical communication inside devices is one approach to these problems.

sections.title: Passing information between light and electronics
sections.body: For example, a signal produced by an electronic circuit can be converted into light, sent through an optical fiber, and converted back into an electrical signal at the receiver. Research and development aim to place the components that perform these conversions close to electronic circuits, or integrate them together.

sections.title: Not every calculation becomes optical
sections.body: Integrating photonics and electronics does not mean replacing all computation with light. Conversion also requires energy and components. Deciding where to transmit information optically and where to process it electronically is an essential part of the design.

ethnography.name: Ethnography
ethnography.introduction: Look beyond what people do to understand what feels ordinary to them.
ethnography.summary: Ethnography involves engaging with people's lives and activities, using observation and dialogue to understand and describe actions and meanings in context. It developed in cultural anthropology and is now also used in fields such as organizational and design research.

sections.title: Entering everyday life
sections.body: Questionnaire answers alone may not reveal everyday behavior or unspoken rules. Researchers spend time in the field, combining participant observation—observing while taking part in activities—with interviews and the examination of records and other materials.

sections.title: What a cup of tea can reveal
sections.body: Consider a workplace tea break. What looks like a simple pause may also be a chance to discuss work or offer advice to a newcomer. This is a fictional illustration: it shows how ethnography asks what an action means in its setting, rather than only counting how often it happens.

sections.title: Questioning the observer's perspective
sections.body: An observation does not automatically become the only truth. An account depends on whom the researcher engaged with and how they interpreted events. Consent, privacy, and reflection on the researcher's own position are essential.

surrealism.name: Surrealism
surrealism.introduction: Let the strangeness of dreams unsettle familiar reality.
surrealism.summary: Surrealism is an artistic and literary movement that explored dreams and the unconscious, seeking expression beyond the limits of reason and convention. André Breton's 1924 Surrealist Manifesto was an important milestone.

sections.title: More than strange paintings
sections.body: Surrealism is known for paintings that combine things in seemingly impossible ways, but it also spread into poetry, writing, photography, and film. Beyond novelty, it questioned ways of seeing reality that are usually taken for granted.

sections.title: Writing before conscious editing
sections.body: One practice was automatic writing: letting words emerge while holding back the impulse to organize them logically or polish the language. It reflected an interest in the unconscious, but the resulting writing should not be treated as a scientific measurement of the mind.

sections.title: New encounters between familiar things
sections.body: An everyday object can take on a different meaning when it appears somewhere unexpected. Surrealism used such encounters and displacements to explore possibilities beyond ordinary arrangements. Methods varied across works and artists.

optical-fiber.name: Optical fiber
optical-fiber.introduction: A thin strand guides light to carry information.
optical-fiber.summary: In optical communication, a fiber that guides light serves as a transmission medium. It is not synonymous with integrating photonics and electronics; it is one technology that supports the transmission of information using light.

ccd.name: CCD
ccd.introduction: How can light become a stored image?
ccd.summary: A CCD collects light-generated charge and transfers it for readout, turning a pattern of light into electrical signals.

sections.title: Understanding the concept
sections.body: In an imaging CCD, pixels collect charge generated by light. Controlled voltages move those charges toward a readout circuit.

sections.title: A concrete example
sections.body: Imagine a grid of rain collectors passing their contents along to one measuring station. This analogy separates collection from readout.

sections.title: Scope and limits
sections.body: Image quality also depends on noise and optics. CMOS sensors are widely used too; digital cameras do not all contain CCDs.

photography.name: Photography
photography.introduction: A way to record light, and a medium for expression.
photography.summary: Photography records light to form images. Here, electronic recording using CCDs and Man Ray's photographic works introduced by MoMA offer two starting points for exploring its technological and artistic aspects.

dada.name: Dada
dada.introduction: What if art questions how art itself is defined?
dada.summary: Dada was an art and literary movement that questioned established values through chance, fragments, and ordinary objects.

sections.title: Understanding the concept
sections.body: Against the background of World War I, artists challenged conventions of making and exhibiting art.

sections.title: A concrete example
sections.body: Consider an everyday object displayed in a museum: what makes it a work? The question shifts attention toward context and institutions.

sections.title: Scope and limits
sections.body: Dada had no single uniform style. Arbitrary making alone does not explain its diverse historical practices.

collage.name: Collage
collage.introduction: Bringing different fragments together into one work.
collage.summary: Collage combines fragments of material, such as pieces of paper. MoMA presents Hans Arp's chance-based collages among the practices associated with Dada.

user-research.name: User research
user-research.introduction: Studying people's behavior and circumstances to inform design decisions.
user-research.summary: One approach visits people in their usual environments and observes their activities. Tools and surroundings help reveal what a service needs to support. User research is not equivalent to ethnography as a whole.

user-centered-design.name: User-centered design (UCD)
user-centered-design.introduction: What changes when design starts with the people using it?
user-centered-design.summary: User-centered design iterates between understanding users, designing, and evaluating whether people can achieve their goals.

sections.title: Understanding the concept
sections.body: Research and evaluation belong throughout design, rather than only at the end. Prototypes help test assumptions about use.

sections.title: A concrete example
sections.body: For a ticket machine, observing destination searches and hands occupied by luggage may suggest changes that a feature request misses.

sections.title: Scope and limits
sections.body: UCD and human-centered design (HCD) are closely related terms. Neither simply means implementing every request or optimizing sales alone.

affordance.name: Affordance
affordance.introduction: What possibilities for action does an environment offer?
affordance.summary: An affordance is a possibility for action arising in the relationship between an environment and an agent.

sections.title: Understanding the concept
sections.body: The same step can afford sitting or climbing differently for different bodies. The unit of analysis is the relationship.

sections.title: A concrete example
sections.body: Imagine a stair climbable by an adult but too high for a toddler. Identical dimensions need not offer identical actions.

sections.title: Scope and limits
sections.body: An available action and a cue making it noticeable can differ. Affordance is broader than a shape that looks clickable.

umwelt.name: Umwelt
umwelt.introduction: Can different creatures inhabit different worlds in one place?
umwelt.summary: Umwelt describes a living being’s meaningful world of perception and action, associated with Jakob von Uexküll.

sections.title: Understanding the concept
sections.body: Organisms attend and respond to different cues. Understanding one requires asking what matters within its perceptual and practical world.

sections.title: A concrete example
sections.body: Imagine walking with a dog: you attend to signs while it stops at scents. A shared street can carry different meanings.

sections.title: Scope and limits
sections.body: We cannot directly inhabit another animal’s experience. The concept invites careful observation, not unrestricted anthropomorphism.

predictive-processing.name: Predictive processing
predictive-processing.introduction: Does the brain perceive by predicting?
predictive-processing.summary: Predictive processing explains perception and learning through predictions about sensory input and the errors those predictions generate.

sections.title: Understanding the concept
sections.body: Prediction errors can update models. How uncertainty is weighted matters; the account is more specific than saying belief creates reality.

sections.title: A concrete example
sections.body: Imagine hearing a familiar order in a noisy café. Contextual expectations can help interpret an ambiguous sound.

sections.title: Scope and limits
sections.body: This is a family of models, not a completed theory of everything the brain does. Illustrations do not establish a neural mechanism.

embodied-cognition.name: Embodied cognition
embodied-cognition.introduction: How do bodies and environments participate in thinking?
embodied-cognition.summary: Embodied cognition is a research program emphasizing the roles of bodies and environmental interaction in cognition.

sections.title: Understanding the concept
sections.body: Bodies can shape how tasks are solved. Researchers disagree about whether bodily contributions merely support cognition or partly constitute it.

sections.title: A concrete example
sections.body: Imagine arranging furniture mentally versus moving small models. Acting on the models changes how comparisons can be made.

sections.title: Scope and limits
sections.body: It does not imply that movement always improves thinking. Claims need a specified task, body, environment, and evidence.

cognitive-dissonance.name: Cognitive dissonance
cognitive-dissonance.introduction: What happens when actions and beliefs conflict?
cognitive-dissonance.summary: Cognitive dissonance is an uncomfortable state associated with inconsistency among relevant cognitions or behavior.

sections.title: Understanding the concept
sections.body: People may reduce dissonance by changing behavior or revising attitudes and interpretations, rather than always choosing one route.

sections.title: A concrete example
sections.body: Imagine making an expensive purchase after deciding to save. One might reinterpret its value or change later spending.

sections.title: Scope and limits
sections.body: Contradictory remarks alone do not diagnose dissonance. Other explanations exist, and another person’s mental state cannot simply be inferred.

exaptation.name: Exaptation
exaptation.introduction: Did a trait originate for the role it plays today?
exaptation.summary: Exaptation describes a trait used for a role for which it was not originally selected.

sections.title: Understanding the concept
sections.body: A feature may be co-opted from another selected function or from a nonadaptive origin. Present usefulness and historical origin are distinct questions.

sections.title: A concrete example
sections.body: Feathers predating flight provide an entry point: their current aerodynamic use alone cannot establish their original role.

sections.title: Scope and limits
sections.body: A history of co-option needs comparative or fossil evidence. An imaginative alternative use does not prove an evolutionary account.

niche-construction.name: Niche construction
niche-construction.introduction: Can organisms change the environments in which they evolve?
niche-construction.summary: Niche construction concerns organisms modifying environments and thereby affecting selection on themselves or other organisms.

sections.title: Understanding the concept
sections.body: Persistent environmental modifications can create ecological inheritance, influencing conditions encountered by later generations.

sections.title: A concrete example
sections.body: A beaver dam changes water flow and habitat conditions. Organismal activity alters conditions for more than its builder.

sections.title: Scope and limits
sections.body: Environmental modification does not automatically demonstrate evolutionary change. Ecological effects and subsequent genetic change require distinct evidence.

neutral-theory.name: Neutral theory of molecular evolution
neutral-theory.introduction: How does chance contribute to molecular evolution?
neutral-theory.summary: Motoo Kimura’s neutral theory emphasizes genetic drift of selectively neutral changes in molecular evolution.

sections.title: Understanding the concept
sections.body: Random sampling across generations can change variant frequencies even without a selective advantage.

sections.title: A concrete example
sections.body: Imagine repeatedly sampling equally likely colored beads to fill the next bag. One color can spread without being superior.

sections.title: Scope and limits
sections.body: The theory does not deny adaptation or claim that every mutation is neutral. Its scope concerns patterns of molecular change.

endosymbiosis.name: Endosymbiotic theory
endosymbiosis.introduction: Do our cells contain descendants of once-independent organisms?
endosymbiosis.summary: Endosymbiotic theory explains the bacterial ancestry of mitochondria and chloroplasts through integration within host cells.

sections.title: Understanding the concept
sections.body: Their DNA, membranes, and evolutionary relationships provide evidence. Modern organelles have become deeply integrated with their hosts.

sections.title: A concrete example
sections.body: Mitochondria involved in cellular energy carry this history. A cell can be understood partly through the integration of lineages.

sections.title: Scope and limits
sections.body: Not every cellular structure has this origin. Details of early integration and eukaryotic origins remain active research questions.

dissipative-structures.name: Dissipative structures
dissipative-structures.introduction: Can a continuing flow of energy sustain order?
dissipative-structures.summary: Dissipative structures are ordered patterns sustained in open systems away from equilibrium through flows of energy or matter.

sections.title: Understanding the concept
sections.body: Stable patterns can be dynamic. Local order is compatible with the second law when exchange with the surroundings is included.

sections.title: A concrete example
sections.body: A fluid heated from below can develop organized convection patterns, sustained by the continuing thermal conditions.

sections.title: Scope and limits
sections.body: Not every flow produces order. Extending the concept to organizations requires care rather than assuming physical laws transfer unchanged.

phase-transition.name: Phase transition
phase-transition.introduction: How can changing conditions transform a whole system?
phase-transition.summary: A phase transition changes a system’s macroscopic state as conditions vary, including changes of state and magnetic ordering.

sections.title: Understanding the concept
sections.body: Interactions among many components produce collective behavior. An order parameter can describe a change at the system level.

sections.title: A concrete example
sections.body: Freezing does not turn water molecules into another molecule. Their collective arrangement and motion change.

sections.title: Scope and limits
sections.body: Transitions differ in character and mechanism. Calling a social change a phase transition needs either a clear model or an explicit metaphor.

emergence.name: Emergence
emergence.introduction: How can interactions produce properties of a whole?
emergence.summary: Emergence concerns novel system-level properties or patterns arising through interactions among components.

sections.title: Understanding the concept
sections.body: Knowing component properties and explaining collective behavior are different tasks. Models can investigate the interactions producing a pattern.

sections.title: A concrete example
sections.body: Imagine people each adjusting distance from the person ahead, producing a moving wave without anyone planning that wave.

sections.title: Scope and limits
sections.body: Emergence is not a substitute for explanation. Practical unpredictability and stronger claims of irreducibility need to be distinguished.

path-dependence.name: Path dependence
path-dependence.introduction: How do past choices shape what can be chosen now?
path-dependence.summary: Path dependence means that outcomes depend on the sequence of earlier events, not only present conditions.

sections.title: Understanding the concept
sections.body: Accumulated skills, equipment, and compatibility can reinforce earlier choices and raise switching costs.

sections.title: A concrete example
sections.body: Imagine a town using one charging connector. A new option may struggle while compatible chargers and users remain scarce.

sections.title: Scope and limits
sections.body: Persistence does not prove inefficiency. Historical influence must be distinguished from current reasons for preferring a system.

transaction-costs.name: Transaction costs
transaction-costs.introduction: Why do firms exist when people can trade in markets?
transaction-costs.summary: Transaction costs include finding partners, negotiating, and enforcing agreements. Coase used them to examine firms and markets.

sections.title: Understanding the concept
sections.body: Trading requires information and coordination beyond the price itself. Internal organization and repeated market contracting have different costs.

sections.title: A concrete example
sections.body: Imagine outsourcing each part of an event separately. Scheduling, communicating changes, and assigning responsibility also consume resources.

sections.title: Scope and limits
sections.body: Internal management has costs too. Organizational boundaries also depend on uncertainty and contracting conditions.

gift-exchange.name: The gift
gift-exchange.introduction: What does a gift create between people?
gift-exchange.summary: Mauss’s account of gifts examines how giving, receiving, and reciprocating are bound up with social relationships and obligations.

sections.title: Understanding the concept
sections.body: Gifts can sustain relationships beyond a single transfer. Expectations of return depend on social context.

sections.title: A concrete example
sections.body: Imagine inviting a friend to dinner after they help you move. Equating hours and food prices misses part of the relationship.

sections.title: Scope and limits
sections.body: This does not reduce generosity to hidden calculation. Obligation, intimacy, and unequal power can coexist in different ways.

liminality.name: Liminality
liminality.introduction: What happens between leaving one status and entering another?
liminality.summary: Liminality describes an in-between phase of transition, developed through studies of rites of passage.

sections.title: Understanding the concept
sections.body: Between separation and incorporation, ordinary distinctions can become unsettled. The transition itself becomes an object of study.

sections.title: A concrete example
sections.body: The interval after graduation but before joining a new institution offers an illustrative entry point into in-betweenness.

sections.title: Scope and limits
sections.body: Not every uncertain period is equivalent to a ritual transition. Broader applications should acknowledge the concept’s anthropological origins.

social-construction.name: Social constructionism
social-construction.introduction: How do social practices establish familiar categories?
social-construction.summary: Social constructionism investigates how meanings and categories depend on social practices, language, and institutions.

sections.title: Understanding the concept
sections.body: A category’s existence does not establish that nature uniquely fixes it. Classification and its consequences can be investigated.

sections.title: A concrete example
sections.body: Consider a paper ticket: its physical properties alone do not explain the institutional right to enter.

sections.title: Scope and limits
sections.body: Social dependence does not mean reality is imaginary or freely changeable. Objects, processes, and material constraints must be specified.

imagined-communities.name: Imagined communities
imagined-communities.introduction: How can strangers imagine belonging to one nation?
imagined-communities.summary: Benedict Anderson examined nations as communities imagined among people who will never meet most fellow members.

sections.title: Understanding the concept
sections.body: Print and shared languages helped shape ways of imagining collective membership. Nationhood becomes a historical question.

sections.title: A concrete example
sections.body: Imagine distant readers treating a dated newspaper’s events as part of their shared society. Meeting is not the only basis of belonging.

sections.title: Scope and limits
sections.body: This is not a single-cause explanation of nation formation. Institutions, colonial histories, and regional differences also matter.

indexicality.name: Indexicality
indexicality.introduction: What does language reveal about the situation of speaking?
indexicality.summary: Indexicality links expressions to the contexts in which they are used: “I,” “here,” and “now” depend on the occasion.

sections.title: Understanding the concept
sections.body: Identical words can refer differently across situations. Sociolinguistic approaches also examine how speech points to social relationships.

sections.title: A concrete example
sections.body: Imagine finding “Meet here tomorrow.” Grammar alone cannot identify the meeting without knowing when and where it was written.

sections.title: Scope and limits
sections.body: Speech does not reliably reveal a speaker’s identity by itself. Social interpretations remain contextual rather than fixed personal classifications.

linguistic-relativity.name: Linguistic relativity
linguistic-relativity.introduction: Can language influence patterns of attention and thought?
linguistic-relativity.summary: Linguistic relativity investigates how language influences thought, without requiring that it completely determines what can be thought.

sections.title: Understanding the concept
sections.body: Languages differ in habitual distinctions. Researchers test how these relate to attention, memory, and other tasks.

sections.title: A concrete example
sections.body: Compare describing positions with left and right versus cardinal directions. The contrast invites questions about habitual attention.

sections.title: Scope and limits
sections.body: A missing word does not prove an inability to understand a concept. Cultural and task differences complicate causal claims.

performativity.name: Performativity
performativity.category: Philosophy of language and social theory
performativity.introduction: Can saying something help bring a social reality into being?
performativity.summary: Austin’s work on speech acts offers an entry into performativity: utterances can do things such as promise or name.

sections.title: Understanding the concept
sections.body: What an utterance says and what it does are distinct questions. Authority, procedures, and circumstances affect whether the act succeeds.

sections.title: A concrete example
sections.body: Imagine an authorized chair declaring a meeting closed. The utterance can participate in ending the meeting.

sections.title: Scope and limits
sections.body: Words do not make any wish real. Later uses, including Butler’s account of gender, require attention to their different theoretical contexts.

paradigm.name: Paradigm
paradigm.introduction: What changes when a scientific community’s shared framework changes?
paradigm.summary: In Kuhn’s philosophy of science, paradigms concern shared exemplars and commitments shaping scientific problems and solutions.

sections.title: Understanding the concept
sections.body: Normal science solves puzzles within shared commitments. Encountering an anomaly and changing a framework are not identical events.

sections.title: A concrete example
sections.body: Imagine learning exemplary solutions in a course. Those examples can shape which new problems seem worth asking.

sections.title: Scope and limits
sections.body: Not every novelty is a paradigm shift. Kuhn’s account does not mean scientific evidence can simply be ignored.

bricolage.name: Bricolage
bricolage.introduction: What can be made by recombining what is already at hand?
bricolage.summary: Lévi-Strauss used bricolage to examine working with an available repertoire of materials and signs.

sections.title: Understanding the concept
sections.body: Knowledge can work by rearranging inherited resources rather than designing every element afresh. Their previous meanings can remain relevant.

sections.title: A concrete example
sections.body: Imagine building a display from old boxes and spare fabric. Existing shapes constrain the design while suggesting unexpected arrangements.

sections.title: Scope and limits
sections.body: The concept is broader than thrift or craft skill. Its anthropological arguments about thought differ from later practical analogies.

rhizome.name: Rhizome
rhizome.introduction: How might connections escape a single center or hierarchy?
rhizome.summary: Deleuze and Guattari developed rhizome as a philosophical concept for multiplicities and connections beyond a single organizing root.

sections.title: Understanding the concept
sections.body: It invites entry from the middle and connections among heterogeneous elements, questioning exhaustive organization under one hierarchy.

sections.title: A concrete example
sections.body: Imagine following a reference from a book to music and then history. Exploration can grow through multiple entry points.

sections.title: Scope and limits
sections.body: Rhizome is not a mathematical measure of networks, nor a guarantee that every decentralized arrangement is desirable.

optical-communication.name: Optical communication
optical-communication.summary: Technology that transmits information using light, including communication through optical fiber.

silicon-photonics.name: Silicon photonics
silicon-photonics.summary: Technology for building small optical circuits and components on a silicon platform.

participant-observation.name: Participant observation
participant-observation.summary: A research method that combines taking part in people's activities with observation to understand practices and meanings in context.

fieldnotes.name: Fieldnotes
fieldnotes.summary: Notes recording events and conversations in the field, alongside the researcher's observations and interpretations.

automatism.name: Automatic writing
automatism.summary: An expressive method of recording words as they arise while holding back conscious editing.

andre-breton.name: André Breton
andre-breton.summary: A French poet and writer who was one of the leading figures of the Surrealist movement.

light.name: Light
light.summary: Light is used both to transmit information and to record images. This does not mean the two uses have the same purpose.

perception-action.name: Perception and action
perception-action.summary: Questions about perception and action can include both bodies and environments.

evolutionary-processes.name: Evolutionary processes
evolutionary-processes.summary: Evolutionary change involves processes including selection and drift across generations.

collective-patterns.name: Collective patterns
collective-patterns.summary: How do component properties and interactions produce system-level behavior?

institutions-norms.name: Institutions and norms
institutions-norms.summary: Social arrangements and expectations shape action and meaning, and can be studied historically.

social-transitions.name: Social relationships and transitions
social-transitions.summary: How do practices establish and transform social relationships and statuses?

utterance-context.name: Context of utterance
utterance-context.summary: The circumstances of speaking include who, when, where, relationships, and procedures.

scientific-community.name: Scientific community
scientific-community.summary: Researchers share questions, methods, and exemplary solutions within communities.

materials-context.name: Materials and context
materials-context.summary: The meanings of objects and signs can change through their arrangement and use.

ethnography-photography.label: One way to document research
ethnography-photography.explanation: Ethnographic practices can use photographs to record and interpret lives and activities. Photographs carry context and the photographer's perspective; photography alone does not replace the whole research process.

surrealism-photography.label: An expressive medium
surrealism-photography.explanation: Surrealism included photographic practices such as photomontage and photograms. Their aims differ from photography used in research. This connection does not claim a direct historical influence between Surrealism and anthropology.

photonics-communication.label: A technology it uses
photonics-communication.explanation: Integrating photonics and electronics combines electronic circuits with optical information transmission. Optical communication supports the transfer of information between and within devices.

photonics-silicon.label: One enabling technology
photonics-silicon.explanation: Silicon photonics integrates optical components at a small scale and is one way to bring light and electronic circuits closer. It does not describe the whole field of integrating photonics and electronics.

ethnography-observation.label: A major research method
ethnography-observation.explanation: Ethnography uses participant observation to understand the context of people's lives and activities. Interviews and examination of documents and other materials are also used.

ethnography-notes.label: A way to record research
ethnography-notes.explanation: Fieldnotes record observed events, conversations, and the researcher's interpretations. Revisiting these records supports description and analysis.

surrealism-automatism.label: An expressive method
surrealism-automatism.explanation: Surrealism explored dreams and the unconscious and practiced automatic writing as one form of expression. This method alone does not explain the entire movement.

breton-surrealism.label: One of the movement's leaders
breton-surrealism.explanation: Breton published the Surrealist Manifesto in 1924 and helped lead the movement, which involved many writers and artists.

photonics-electronics--light.label: Used to transmit information
photonics-electronics--light.explanation: Integrating photonics and electronics combines optical input and output with electronic circuits.

optical-fiber--optical-communication.label: Provides a transmission medium
optical-fiber--optical-communication.explanation: Optical fiber guides light as a transmission medium in optical communication.

ccd--light.label: Detects light for recording
ccd--light.explanation: A CCD is a semiconductor imaging circuit that captures light electronically.

photography--light.label: Records it as an image
photography--light.explanation: Electronic photography uses imaging sensors such as CCDs to capture light.

photography--ccd.label: One electronic recording method
photography--ccd.explanation: CCDs are one technology used to record photographs electronically.

dada--collage.label: One expressive method
dada--collage.explanation: MoMA presents collage among Dada's methods, including Hans Arp's chance-based work.

dada--photography.label: Uses photographic fragments too
dada--photography.explanation: Dada includes photomontage, which combines fragments of photographs.

user-research--participant-observation.label: Uses observation in context
user-research--participant-observation.explanation: User research can also observe activities in everyday settings. The degree of participation varies across studies; the two methods are not identical.

user-research--fieldnotes.label: Records observations in context
user-research--fieldnotes.explanation: GOV.UK's contextual research guidance describes recording what is seen and heard in notes. Recording also supports analysis in ethnography.

user-centered-design--user-research.label: Deepens understanding of users
user-centered-design--user-research.explanation: The GOV.UK Service Standard calls for user research to understand what people need when designing a service.

affordance--perception-action.label: Possibilities for action
affordance--perception-action.explanation: Affordances relate possibilities for action to an agent and its environment.

umwelt--perception-action.label: Meaning for an organism
umwelt--perception-action.explanation: Umwelt asks what matters within an organism’s world of perception and action.

predictive-processing--perception-action.label: Predictions and sensory errors
predictive-processing--perception-action.explanation: Predictive processing studies perception and action through predictions and prediction errors.

embodied-cognition--perception-action.label: Roles of body and environment
embodied-cognition--perception-action.explanation: Embodied cognition investigates contributions of sensorimotor activity and environment to cognition.

exaptation--evolutionary-processes.label: Origin versus current use
exaptation--evolutionary-processes.explanation: Exaptation distinguishes present use from an account of selection for that use.

niche-construction--evolutionary-process.label: Changing selective environments
niche-construction--evolutionary-process.explanation: Organisms can modify selective environments, with effects across generations.

neutral-theory--evolutionary-processes.label: Drift in molecular change
neutral-theory--evolutionary-processes.explanation: Neutral theory emphasizes drift of neutral variants in molecular evolution.

endosymbiosis--evolutionary-processes.label: Origins through integration
endosymbiosis--evolutionary-processes.explanation: Endosymbiotic theory examines organelle origins through integration of hosts and bacteria.

dissipative-structures--collective-patte.label: Order sustained by flows
dissipative-structures--collective-patte.explanation: Flows and dissipation can sustain ordered patterns away from equilibrium.

phase-transition--collective-patterns.label: System changes with conditions
phase-transition--collective-patterns.explanation: A phase transition changes a macroscopic state as conditions vary.

emergence--collective-patterns.label: Wholes arising from interactions
emergence--collective-patterns.explanation: Emergence asks about collective properties, interactions, and levels of description.

path-dependence--institutions-norms.label: History of institutions
path-dependence--institutions-norms.explanation: Path dependence examines persistence through earlier choices and accumulated investments.

transaction-costs--institutions-norms.label: Arrangements supporting exchange
transaction-costs--institutions-norms.explanation: Transaction costs illuminate differences between markets and organizations.

social-construction--institutions-norms.label: How categories are established
social-construction--institutions-norms.explanation: Social construction investigates categories through practices, language, and institutions.

imagined-communities--institutions-norms.label: Imagining shared membership
imagined-communities--institutions-norms.explanation: Imagined communities asks about historical conditions of shared national membership.

gift-exchange--social-transitions.label: Relationships through gifts
gift-exchange--social-transitions.explanation: Gifts can sustain obligations and relationships beyond the transfer of an object.

liminality--social-transitions.label: Between social statuses
liminality--social-transitions.explanation: Liminality concerns the phase between statuses in transitions such as rites of passage.

indexicality--utterance-context.label: Context-dependent meaning
indexicality--utterance-context.explanation: Expressions such as “I,” “here,” and “now” vary in reference across contexts.

performativity--utterance-context.label: When uttering is acting
performativity--utterance-context.explanation: Promises and declarations depend on appropriate circumstances and procedures.

linguistic-relativity--utterance-context.label: Language and cognition
linguistic-relativity--utterance-context.explanation: Beyond context-dependent reference, linguistic relativity asks how linguistic habits influence cognition.

paradigm--scientific-community.label: Shared exemplars and commitments
paradigm--scientific-community.explanation: Kuhn connects scientific practice with exemplars and commitments shared in a community.

bricolage--materials-context.label: Reworking existing resources
bricolage--materials-context.explanation: Bricolage recombines resources that retain traces of earlier uses and meanings.

rhizome--materials-context.label: Connections in many directions
rhizome--materials-context.explanation: Rhizome is a philosophical way of considering connections beyond a single central hierarchy.

cognitive-dissonance--institutions-norms.label: Beliefs and behavior in conflict
cognitive-dissonance--institutions-norms.explanation: Social expectations and behavior can conflict. This comparison does not explain individual psychology solely from institutions.

affordance--embodied-cognition.label: Two perspectives on body and environment
affordance--embodied-cognition.explanation: Both offer entry points into body–environment relations, without making ecological psychology and embodied cognition identical.

umwelt--affordance.label: Comparing organism–environment relations
umwelt--affordance.explanation: Umwelt concerns meaningful worlds; affordances concern possibilities for action. They are related questions, not synonyms.

predictive-processing--embodied-cognitio.label: A meeting point for accounts of cognition
predictive-processing--embodied-cognitio.explanation: Some research brings these approaches together; their relationship varies with theoretical interpretation.

phase-transition--emergence.label: Comparing collective changes and properties
phase-transition--emergence.explanation: Collective changes offer an entry into emergence, without implying that all emergence is a phase transition.

path-dependence--transaction-costs.label: Switching and coordination costs
path-dependence--transaction-costs.explanation: Switching can involve contracting and coordination costs. These concepts illuminate different aspects of persistence.

social-construction--imagined-communitie.label: Social formation of membership
social-construction--imagined-communitie.explanation: Historical national membership offers a case for asking how social categories form, without equating the two accounts.

bricolage--rhizome.label: Comparing recombination and connections
bricolage--rhizome.explanation: Recombination and noncentral connections can be compared; this edge claims neither synonymy nor direct influence.
